text: Back in early twenty twenty-three, if you asked ChatGPT what was on in London that weekend, it would apologise. It couldn't browse the internet, and its knowledge stopped at a date. Ask the same question today, and you'll see a little line that says searching the web. A few seconds later, you've got events, with dates and links.

The model got better too. But it still can't search on its own. Somebody built software around it. And that software is what turns an LLM into an agent. In the last topic, we looked at the model itself. You give it text, and it predicts the next token, then the next, until the answer is done. Its knowledge stops on the day

training stopped. And on its own, it can't open a browser, or a file, or look anything up. Text in, text out. So an agent is that same model, with three things wrapped around it: context, tools, and a loop. Start with context. Say we call the model directly, with no app around it, and type:

hi, I'm Sara, and I live in San Francisco. Then, in the next message, we ask for her name. It has no idea. Every call starts from nothing. So the app sends the earlier messages back in, with every new one. On the first turn, the request holds one message. By the fifth, it's carrying the

whole conversation. That bundle is the context: everything the model sees on one call. The instructions, the history, the tool descriptions, the results. It's the agent's entire world. And most of the time, when an agent seems dumb, the context is wrong: too little, too much, or the wrong stuff.

Now, back to London. The model still can't search. But it can say that it wants to. Along with your question, the app sends a short description of a web search tool, and when to use it. The model reads that. And instead of answering, it replies with a request: search for events in London this week. The app runs that search, not the

model. It pastes the results into the context, and calls the model again. Now the model has real, current results in front of it, so it answers from those. So a tool is two pieces: the code the app runs, and a short description, so the model knows the tool exists. And because the app runs it, the app

decides whether it should run at all. That's where permissions and safety live. Look at what just happened. The model asked for something, the app did it, and the result went back in, so the model could decide what to do next. Do that over and over, and you have an agent loop: read, plan, act, observe, repeat.

The London question takes a round or two. Ask it to build a one-page website, and it goes around many times. It builds a bit, looks at the result, fixes it, and goes again. So you cap the steps, or it can go in circles. And you set rules for when to stop and ask a person. Some restaurants take phone orders with AI

now. If someone orders two hundred and fifty milkshakes, that order goes to a human. So here's all of it on one screen. In the middle, the model, and it only writes text. Around it, the context: everything we send on each call. Next to it, the tools, which the app runs when the model asks.

Then the rules about what it may do on its own, like that milkshake rule. And around everything, the loop that keeps it going. Everything around the model is called the harness. ChatGPT is a harness around a model. Claude Code is another one, built for writing software. Under this video, step through one full turn

of that loop for Parcelly, a small delivery company, one step at a time. Then, in your steps, give Claude Code a customer's question about an order. Watch what it reads and what it decides before it answers. Then ask it to walk you back through what it did: read, plan, act, observe.
In Module 3, you'll build this loop yourself. Next, we open up Claude Code and look inside its harness.
